gloss: love · cherish · regard — and, in Buddhist texts, craving
formNote: Earlier written 㤅: 心 “heart” with 旡 as phonetic. The foot 夊 was added from the Qin period on, and the top later reshaped into 爫 + 冖. Reading 旡 as a figure “turning back in regard” is interpretive.
summary: Love, cherishing, regard, with a heart (心) at the centre of the graph. In Buddhist translation the same character also renders tṛṣṇā, the thirst the tradition diagnoses — which is why precision matters here.
placement: High on the right wing, beside 二 — the two ends of the Maitrādvaita proposition.

readings.extraNote: Readings beyond Unihan’s list, added by Baracus from general knowledge; not yet checked.

satellites.title: A Heart, Then Feet
satellites.evidence: The Shuowen glosses 㤅 as “kindness” (惠) and 愛 as a manner of walking (行皃): the foot 夊 belongs to the second graph, which absorbed the first. The heart stayed at the centre.

satellites.title: Craving vs. Loving-Kindness
satellites.evidence: Among the twelve links, 愛 translates tṛṣṇā, “thirst, craving”. Loving-kindness, maitrī, is usually 慈 — first of the Four Immeasurables 慈悲喜捨 — and is distinct from karuṇā (悲), the wish that beings be free from suffering.
satellites.caveat: 愛 is not the standard rendering of maitrī.

satellites.title: Impartial Care vs. Graded Love
satellites.evidence: Mohists argued for 兼愛, care extended to all equally. Mencius attacked it as denying the special claim of one’s own father, defending a love graded outward from family — the Confucian 仁, later often called 仁愛.

satellites.title: Tender Care vs. Passion
satellites.evidence: Malay distinguishes kasih and sayang (tender, protective affection) from berahi (passionate desire) — a split comparable to Greek agapē and philia versus erōs.

satellites.title: Maitrādvaita — a Proposition
satellites.evidence: Proposed reading: where the line between self and other is seen through (不二, advaya), care for others may arise as naturally as care for oneself.
satellites.caveat: It sits near — but is not identical to — the Mahāyāna pairing of wisdom (prajñā) with compassion (karuṇā). No canonical text defines 不二 this way.
satellites.statusNote: Wording awaits Ben’s decision (roadmap: Decisions Only Ben Can Make).

satellites.title: Love Without a Heart
satellites.lang: Modern Chinese — a joke about simplification
satellites.evidence: Simplified 爱 drops the 心 at the centre of 愛 and writes 友, “friend”, in its place. A couplet by 夏進興 makes the joke: 麵無麥、愛無心、單翅能飛 / 餘不食、親不見、無門可開 — noodles without wheat, love without a heart, one wing that still flies; surplus without food, kin who cannot see, no gate yet it opens.
satellites.caveat: A joke, not an etymology. Simplified forms were chosen for ease of writing, often by regularising older cursive handwriting, not to take meaning out. The couplet speaks for one side of a long and political debate.

checked.note: 麵無麥、愛無心、單翅能飛 / 餘不食、親不見、無門可開
